item.description:
• The frame rate stays at 30 whenever the window can be seen, focused or not: a desk toy sits beside the work, and dropping to 8 the moment it lost focus made it lag in the corner of the eye. Only a covered or hidden window goes to 8
  • The plan draws its dead-end alleys off the long arms again, every few runs, two or three tiles, on the side the arm last jogged away from, reserved like the arms and dug whole when a room wants the frontage; the passages between arms stay demand-dug. Judged on the forty and eighty room fills (RK_FILL=1 prints both, with mean walk, loops and footprint), that gives the crinkle back and a tighter footprint at the same mean walk. Charging the arms more past six steps and doubling the passage bonus changed nothing, so those knobs stay at their defaults. RK_FPS prints the frame rate the view is actually running at, which is how the low rate while hidden was checked: ten frames a second. A snapshot says how many nodes with geometry the scene holds
  • A desk toy's diet: the audio engine is stopped outright while music is off, where it rendered silence forty times a second; the frame rate is 30 when watched, 60 only while a gesture drives the camera, and 8 while the window is covered or the app is in the background; antialiasing is 2X, which reads the same as 4X on flat shading and straight edges. The debug build went from 62% of a core to about 12%

• The order in hand owns the body's posture, in the model and in the picture. A new order of another kind drops the old one's leftovers: the spot it was shuffling to, the seat, the bench, the fixture it held, the towel, and a visit's place goes back to where the visit began; so a job that cuts in on the way to the gym or the bath takes the body clean, where before each such crossing had its own bug, the runner at the console, the tester on the treadmill, the reaction in the bath. The picture draws the bath's pixels and the water from the bath order in hand, not from the place flag, and the working pose yields to a job as well as to a visit. A sim test cuts in on both kinds of visit and checks nothing is left on the body
  • The bay is five wide with the slots two tiles apart, so nobody at one slot is ever within a tile of the next and the rush of arrivals runs clean. A visit outranks the day's work in the picture: a busy worker sent to the gym was drawn testing with the scanner out on the treadmill; on a fixture the hands are empty and the workout's pose is the pose
  • Hallway once dug is reserved for good: a room could be placed across an alley dug for an earlier room, since only the planned arms were held back. The fade-in of new floor is capped at a couple of seconds, so a burst of digging no longer leaves tiles unseen for as long as it took. --layout-tests holds that no room stands on the hallway
  • The bay under a rush of arrivals. Twelve branches two seconds apart exhausted the three slots, and the fallback set a ship down on a slot that still had a crate and its carrier: a ship now holds high over the bay until its slot is clear, of any earlier order still to be fetched, of any other ship over it, and of anyone within a tile of it but its own carrier or passenger. The bay is three deep: ships land on the back row, a carrier waits on the middle row a full tile in front of its slot and takes the last arm's length from there rather than from a neighbouring slot's side, and the front row is the way in from the hatch. A worker out of one shuttle stands by it while another is coming down. The check that nobody walks under a shuttle spares a crate's own carrier, who stands within reach on purpose, and names positions and errands when it fires. The ships step with their list untouched, since a ship's clearance reads the others. The twelve-branch simulator script runs clean of violations and give-ups
  • A worker out of one shuttle stands by it while another shuttle with a worker is coming down or unloading on the next slot, then walks in: on the three-slot bay the way to the hatch passes under the middle slot, and the check that nobody walks under a shuttle said so. A carrier on a job keeps its own wait for its crate's ship
  • The hallway is dug as rooms arrive rather than drawn ahead. The plan keeps only the skeleton, the plaza and the four arms; the alleys off them and the passages between them come from the rooms: for each new room every place it could go is weighed against the hallway as built plus one dig, the next cells of an arm, a dead-end alley off any hallway cell, or the shortest passage through free floor to hallway far away by walking, and scored by the room's walk to the bay and the deck, half a step per cell dug, half a step back per free tile the dig opens a door onto, and a bonus for a passage; the least wins, ties by steps from the plaza and then the lowest cell, so two machines with the same rooms dig the same hallway. An alley may cross an arm's unbuilt cells, which are hallway either way. The dug hallway is saved with the station and new floor fades in by the order it was dug. A pallet ordered while someone was on the treadmill sent them running on the spot by the console: a visit is not a job, so the picker took them, and the walk was given to a body whose order had only been queued; visitors are left to their turn and only a body whose order began walks. --layout-tests prints the mean walk from a door to the plaza for the forty-room fill; --sim-tests holds the pallet order to waiting for the turn to end
  • Shortcuts in the plan: every other alley is a loop rather than a dead end, out three tiles, along the arm four to six and back into it further on, so the hallway is a web of ways round with a two-wide strip of room frontage inside each loop. The alleys themselves had never been drawn: the clearance check counted the arm's own tiles beside the base as other hallway and refused every one, which is also why the forty-room fill ran the arms out so far; the check now spares only the straight run through the base, and an alley tries the arm's other side when its first is blocked. A reaction that arrived mid-shower waited its turn and then began standing in the bath with no walk planned, the pixels still on; a queued reaction now gets its walk the moment the visit ends. The shuttle's own passenger is under it by nature and no longer trips the check, and an arrival stands by the ship for the second it takes to lift off rather than walking out from under it. --layout-tests holds the hallway to having loops; --sim-tests holds the reaction to walking off after the shower
  • The station leaves the cross. The hallway is a Plan drawn once from the station's name: a plaza three by three round the monolith, four arms one tile wide, the west and south ones fixed so the yard and the bay never move, the north and east ones wandering outward in runs and jogs with short alleys off them, built on in steps as rooms need frontage; every cell of the plan is reserved whether built or not, so no room ever stands where hallway will run. A room goes on the free frontage fewest hallway steps from the plaza, alleys before the next stretch of arm, so the station fills outward along the way people walk. The airlock is a chamber one wide and two deep, the bay three wide with a slot per column, the hallway meets the deck at one door and the yard's own aisles stay two wide for the pallet. New floor fades in by the step it was built at. --layout-tests gains the hallway in one piece, the arms and alleys keeping apart, and a forty-room fill drawn as text so the growth can be read without a window; the scenario suite passes on the new floor without a change to any scenario. STATION.md, ARCHITECTURE.md and LAYOUT.md say so; the fleet file is v21
  • An office's shape follows its key through the stable hash, so a room looks the same on every launch and on every machine; it came from Swift's own hashValue, which is seeded afresh per process, so the same office drew a different shape each time it was placed anew. The tool rota's seed goes the same way. --layout-tests holds the floor plan to being a pure function of shared facts: two stations given the same rooms in the same order lay them out cell for cell the same, the same key takes the same cells twice, and every room has a door on the corridor and keeps off the yard. LAYOUT.md is the plan for what comes next: the wandering one-wide hallway with alleys, the 3x3 plaza round the monolith, rooms of three to seven tiles placed along the hallway, the game's palette kept beside ours, a minion scale behind a setting, and the peer tie-break that makes a shared station converge; with the order of work and the decisions taken

• build.sh looks for the release product in .build/out, where the native build system lays out a universal build; the old .build/apple path was left over from Xcode's own layout and made every release say the build failed
  • The camera can go with one minion: a click follows it, keeping it in the middle while the zoom and the turn stay yours, with its order written along the bottom in its own words; Esc, a pan or a click on the floor lets go, and a double-click now does what a click did, asking GitHub again. A shower ends at the towel rail: the towel comes off the rail onto the shoulders for a few seconds, the water stops, and it goes back; the rail itself moved to the far end of the wall so it no longer reads as the nozzle from the camera's angle. The simulator's clock is two rows, pause and step as icons and the speeds under them, and the quarter and half buttons no longer light up with 1x. Headless runs ignore a cursor left over a minion, which is what froze a sitter in front of the bowl on film. For filming: --look frames a room, --follow keeps the camera on a minion, --frames and --every take a strip of pictures. AUDIT.md is re-checked against the simulation split, cited by function rather than line, with 18 rows moved upward and the open items kept; STATION.md's shower length matches the code. --sim-tests gains the bath's reservation, the sit on arrival and the drying beat
  • build.sh removes last time's binary before compiling, so a failed compile says so instead of bundling the stale one
  • The repo folder is ~/dev/rumkapsel now, and the demo station's entry for it says so too
  • The long idle run is gone, and the rule it kept tripping: what it watched, that visits happen in a mix and last their whole time, the idle tests and the sim tests check in seconds, and two minions standing on one spot is no longer a rule of the station. The little disorder in storage and on an office's boxes is seeded from a hash that is the same in every run, where Swift's own hashValue was seeded afresh per process. The docs say where things stand: TESTING.md opens with the gate as one block to run, ARCHITECTURE.md's debts are the debts there are, and README.md says how to test and how to release, and that notarisation needs credentials stored once. The builds name the native build system: Xcode 26.1's default lays the products out where the debug binary cannot find Sparkle beside it
